items.followUp: What is the difference between elastic and plastic deformation?

rubric.why: The definition must state both the recovery of the original shape and that this happens when the deforming force is removed.
rubric.description: Defines the elastic limit by the body's ability to recover its original shape after removal of the deforming force.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for both key ideas; award 1 mark if only one is given or the meaning is partly correct.

modelAnswer: The elastic limit is the maximum limit up to which a body returns to its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed.

items.followUp: Write the formula for density and volume.

rubric.why: Pressure is defined as force per unit area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula in words or symbols.

rubric.why: Strain is the ratio of change in length to original length.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula in words or symbols.

modelAnswer: Pressure = force / area, or P = F/A.
Strain = change in length / original length, or strain = ΔL/L.

items.followUp: What is meant by the temperature of a body?

rubric.why: Internal energy is the sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies.
rubric.description: Defines internal energy as the total energy of the molecules of a substance.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for identifying both molecular kinetic and potential energy; award 1 mark for identifying either one.

modelAnswer: The internal energy of a substance is the total kinetic and potential energy of its molecules.
The kinetic energy is due to the random motion of the molecules, and the potential energy is due to the forces between them.

items.followUp: State Newton’s second law of motion and give one example.

rubric.why: The law describes the persistence of rest or uniform straight-line motion unless an unbalanced external force acts.
rubric.description: States Newton’s first law of motion.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete law; award 1 mark for a substantially correct but incomplete statement.

rubric.why: These examples illustrate inertia: an object's state of motion or rest tends to persist.
rubric.description: Gives one suitable example, such as a passenger moving forward when a bus stops suddenly or dust falling from a beaten carpet.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correctly described example.

rubric.why: The question asks for two examples demonstrating Newton’s first law.
rubric.description: Gives a second suitable example of inertia.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second distinct, correctly described example.

modelAnswer: Newton’s first law states that a body remains at rest or continues to move with uniform speed in a straight line unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force.
When a moving bus stops suddenly, a passenger tends to move forward because the body tends to continue in motion.
When a carpet is beaten, dust particles fall off because they tend to remain at rest while the carpet moves.

items.followUp: Define kinetic energy and derive its equation.

rubric.why: Potential energy is energy possessed by a body because of its position or configuration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating potential energy to position or configuration.

rubric.why: A suitable example shows energy associated with position.
rubric.description: Gives an example of potential energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example, such as a raised body or water stored in a dam.

rubric.why: The derivation uses the lifting force equal to the body's weight and work done equal to force times distance.
rubric.description: Sets up the work done in raising a mass through height h.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the lifting force as mg and the distance as h.

rubric.why: The work done against gravity is stored as gravitational potential energy.
rubric.description: Obtains the equation for gravitational potential energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for deriving or stating PE = mgh.

modelAnswer: Potential energy is the energy possessed by a body because of its position or configuration.
For example, a raised body has gravitational potential energy.
To raise a body of mass m through a height h, the force applied against gravity is equal to its weight: F = mg.
Work done = force × distance = mg × h = mgh.
This work is stored as potential energy; therefore, PE = mgh.

items.followUp: State Pascal’s law and explain how it is used in a hydraulic machine.

rubric.why: Pascal’s law says that pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished throughout the liquid and in every direction.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete principle; award 1 mark if transmission of pressure is stated but the principle is incomplete.

rubric.why: The hydraulic press works because equal pressure acts on both pistons: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
rubric.description: Applies Pascal’s law to the two pistons of a hydraulic press.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the pressure relation or its correct verbal equivalent.

rubric.why: A larger output piston produces a larger force for the same transmitted pressure.
rubric.description: Explains how the press multiplies force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that a small force on the small piston can lift a large load on the larger piston.

modelAnswer: Pascal’s law states that pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions throughout the liquid.
A hydraulic press has two pistons of different areas connected by an enclosed liquid.
By Pascal’s law, the pressures at the two pistons are equal: P₁ = P₂, so F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
Since the area of the larger piston is greater, it exerts a larger force and can lift a heavy load.

items.followUp: Name any four derived quantities and give their SI units.

rubric.why: The SI system has seven base quantities; any four correctly named quantities satisfy the question.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for four correct names; award 1 mark for two or three correct names.

modelAnswer: Four base quantities are length, mass, time and electric current.
